preamble: Palatalization of the alveolar implosive [ɗ] to the glottalized palatal approximant [jˀ] (also transcribed [ʔʲ]), Hausa ʼy (written ƴ in Niger). Newman (1996: 539) calls Hausa /ʼy/ a historically recent phoneme, found in only a few very high frequency words, that developed from the sequence /ɗiy-/ via /ɗy/; Western Hausa keeps ɗìyaa 'daughter' where Standard Hausa has ʼyaa. Schuh & Yalwa (1993: 79), who transcribe the sound [ʔʲ] and describe it as a palatalized glottal stop often considered a glottalized palatal, likewise call it a contraction of [ɗij] (Sokoto [ɗìjaː] vs Kano [ʔʲaː] 'daughter'); Ladefoged and Wikipedia write it [j̰]. Wikipedia, citing Newman (2000: 397), also derives it from palatalized ɗ. In the Bade–Ngizim group, Schuh (2002) describes an active process in Ngizim and Duwai that palatalizes alveolars before -i in certain morphological environments, under which ɗ alternates with ʼy ('eat meat'). Because that alternation is morphologically conditioned, it is not marked as allophony. Schuh also lists Western Bade ɗyàwu against Gashua Bade and Ngizim ʼyàwu 'give birth' and describes the group's palatal glottals as [ɗy] or [ʼy]; he gives no direction for that pair. The statements are explicit, but each language supplies only one or two words.

examples.note: Newman (1996: 539): /ʼy/ developed "from the sequence /ɗiy-/ via /ɗy/", so the Western form keeps the older shape. Wiktionary calls ʼyā a syncopic form of ɗìyā, citing Newman (2000: 229). Ladefoged transcribes the word [j̰aː]. The sources consulted give only this one example.
